Canadian Camping 



ONE ASPECT 


of Staff Supervision 
in Camp 


ALAN KLEIN, 

School of Social Work, University of Toronto 


Not much has been written about 
supervision in camp, although there 
is copious material on staff supervision 
in allied fields. Dr. Hedley Dimock’s 
chapter in “Administration of the Mod¬ 
em Camp” is one of the most compre¬ 
hensive statements yet written, although 
he, himself, indicates the need to adopt 
the techniques of group work super¬ 
vision to the camp situation. Too few 
of us have the oportunity to do that. 
Many camp people feel reluctant to 
use supervision in its fullest sense in 
camp. This is partly due to the fact 
that the word has unfortunate conno¬ 
tations in the mind of the average 
person. 

Many feel that supervision implies 
a formal boss or foreman type relation¬ 
ship. Overseeing or spying, or worse, 
telling the staff member what and how 
to do his job and demanding rigid con¬ 
formance. This is not what is meant. 

Supervision of staff in camp is per¬ 
haps more important than in many 
other fields where it is more readily 
accepted—the average camp today em¬ 
ploys untrained and often young and 
inexperienced staff. We have rendered 
lip-service to the importance of the 
counselor in helping camping to reach 
its most honoured objectives. The coun¬ 
selor is the key person in camp. It is 
he who aids the growth and develop¬ 


ment of the camper. To help those 
counselors do an effective job is per¬ 
haps the most important single func¬ 
tion of administration. 

Supervision implies that we, with 
greater experience and preparation, 
are responsible for helping the counselor 
with less experience and equipment 
to develop his abilities to do a more 
effective job, derive satisfaction from 
the job, and develop into a first-class 
staff person. The supervisor is respon¬ 
sible to see that a good job is done with 
the campers and also to see that his 
staff is trained to increasingly develop 
greater skills for the job. 

Many camp directors have privately 
and publicly expressed the idea that 
there is little time in camp for super¬ 
vision. A camp that runs at such a 
tempo or is so understaffed that there 
is no time for staff growth can have 
little time for camper growth. 

The subject of supervision to be ade¬ 
quately treated here would take many 
pages. The only aspects mentioned, 
therefore, will be how and why of 
staff relations. 

The camp supervisor, i.e., head coun¬ 
selor, personnel director, program di¬ 
rector, or executive, has as his first big 
job the establishment of good relation¬ 
ships with his staff. He must by word 


Tor onto 9 Canada , June, 1949 


7 


and act convince them that he is inter¬ 
ested in helping the counselor to do a 
good job. He must get across the idea 
that he is not criticizing, not being 
judgmental, but is concerned with the 
campers and staff to bring about the 
objectives of the camp and also for 
everyone to have an enjoyable and 
worthwhile experience. This implies 
that the supervisor must feel that way. 
He must be able to accept and like 
people, to recognize and give credit to 
the points of view of other staff mem¬ 
bers and to make them feel needed and 
valuable. They are people who will 
discuss problems with staff members, 
permitting and enabling them to think 
for themselves. That is the key to good 
supervision. 

More often than not, it is the atti¬ 
tudes of the counselor that are of con¬ 
cern. Perhaps he is too authoritative 
or perhaps we think he is lazy. Both 
are attitudes and must be worked out. 
People do not learn to change by being 
told to or even by having the reason¬ 
ableness and logic of another attitude 
explained to them. Learning can, how T - 
ever, come through experience and 
sympathetic discussion of the way we 
do things. 

Supervision of staff in camp involves 
certain things that are not technical 
and do not require the skill of a trained 
expert. The first is the establishment 
of a good relationship. This implies 
that the counselor is made to feel that 
he can discuss problems, present sug¬ 
gestions and count on getting help. 
Regular opportunities for private dis¬ 
cussions with the supervisor arc essen¬ 
tial. To say that the supervisor will be 
available if needed is not sufficient, for 
often the person who needs it most is 
the last one to come. If staff are en¬ 
couraged to come regularly, there is 
no feeling that one comes only if there 
are problems, or for a “talking to”. 

The supervisor helps to keep the con¬ 
ference going by asking a few ques¬ 


tions, making a suggestion here and 
there and getting the counselor to 
either advance a solution, get it oft' his 
chest, or perhaps get assurance that 
he is doing a good job. Often that 
which is unsaid reveals the counselor’s 
feelings and a wise supervisor, by asking 
a question or two, can bring to light 
what is beneath the surface. He should 
be a good listener and give only such 
information as is necessary to stimulate 
thinking. He encourages, praises, and 
builds up his staff. He looks behind 
the deed to determine the reason for 
laziness, failure, inability to get his 
group to like him, etc., and seeks to get 
these things discussed. He guides the 
discussion through, knowing as much as 
he can about his counselor and by 
having an objective. He seeks to en¬ 
able his staff person to do his job. He 
knows that staff have fears, and anxie¬ 
ties about the job, and that there must 
be a chance to release these tensions— 
and above all, he knows that a relaxed 
camp comes from relaxed staff. 

I have not said much about tech¬ 
niques, skills in observation, etc. The 
basic skill to be learned is that of de¬ 
veloping our own attitudes. It is easy 
to talk and tell the counselor what to 
do. It makes us feel good to show that 
we know the answers and can glibly 
rattle off solutions. It is easy to be so 
important, so knowledgable, and so 
ready that we stifle all initiative on 
the part of the staff. It is easy to be 
authoritative and be the administrator 
who hands out policy. Attitudes cannot 
be changed that way and counselors will 
not reveal to such supervisors the prob¬ 
lems about which they need the most 
help. We must school ourselves to be 
interested and sympathetic, warm and 
helpful. It is the humility of the 
teacher and his desire to work with 
rather than over or on, that establishes a 
supervisory relationship resulting in 
learning, growth, and above all—good 
camping. 


8 


Canadian Camping 



Bolton Camp 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1949 


9 


Counselor Responsibilities 

for HEALTH in CAMP 

J. H. EBBS, M.D., M.R.C.P. (Lond.), F.R.C.P.(C) 

Medical Director, Taylor Statten Camps 


Reprinted in part from 
“CAMPING MAGAZINE” June, 40. 


Few will disagree with the statement 
that parents send their children to camp 
to have a good time in a healthy and 
safe environment. Thus, health is one 
of camping’s main objectives. If good 
health is not improved or at least main¬ 
tained, then the camp experience has, 
in most instances, been a failure. 

The trend in medical practice among 
children is towards a preventive out¬ 
look? This trend is becoming more 
widespread in the medical arrangement 
of organized camps everywhere, and 
is in contrast with the old idea of 
treating things after they have oc¬ 
curred. 

The responsibility for putting the 
health of the camp on a preventive 
basis rests with two divisions of the 
camp personnel: (a) the Medical Staff 
—Doctor and Nurse; (b) the Camp 
Staff—Director and Counselors. 

RESPONSIBILITY OF THE 
MEDICAL STAFF 

(1) A report of a medical examina¬ 
tion by the camper’s own physician, 
together with all the facts which might 
be important in the event of any con¬ 
dition arising while the child is at 
camp, should be sent to the camp phy¬ 


sician just before the opening date. 
An examination and report more than 
a week before camp opens, loses a great 
deal of its preventive value. A physi¬ 
cian who has been supervising the 
health of the child previously, can give 
valuable advice regarding special and 
important points for insuring optimum 
health for the individual camper. 

(2) A superficial medical examina¬ 
tion can usually be made by the camp 
physician at the point of embarkation 
for camp, on the train to camp, or at 
the point where campers meet to enroll 
in the camp. If this is done before 
campers have mixed and come in too 
close contact with each other, it has a 
preventive value in eliminating early 
cases of infectious conditions. For 
example — an examination of the 
mouth, throat, tongue, inside of the 
cheeks, and the skin of the neck and 
arms, will take only a few moments 
to carry out, but it will serve to detect 
infectious conditions which could be 
spread during the close contact neces¬ 
sary in travel and at the opening of 
camp. 

(3) A regular complete physical 
examination of each camper by the 
doctor should be carried out during the 
first day. 


10 


Canadian Camping 


(4) Information regarding special 
care, special needs, requests from fam¬ 
ily physician and parents, diets, serum 
injections, rest, etc., should be com¬ 
piled as early as possible by the doctor, 
and given to each member of the staff 
who will have responsibility for the 
camper—(Counselor, swimming direc¬ 
tor, dietitian, riding instructor, etc.). 
Much of this information can be sent 
out or at least prepared before the 
opening of camp. It is embarassing to 
find that in the rush of opening days 
in camp, some important medical or 
dietary instructions have been over¬ 
looked for a week or more. 

(5) Records of weight kept by the 
medical staff should be made at fre¬ 
quent intervals to check and guide 
camp activity for the individual 
camper. 

(6) Sanitary inspections should be 
under the direction of the medical 
staff. 

RESPONSIBILITY OF 
CAMP STAFF 

The activities of each camper 
throughout the 24 hour period are 
under the guidance and supervision 
of the staff. Here the counselor serves 
as the most important single force in 
determining whether or not preventive 
measures arc practiced in the daily 
routine of the camper. A few brief 
notes are listed upon some of the points 
which deserve consideration by a first- 
rate counselor. 

(1) Daily Inspection — A thorough 
daily inspection by the counselor of 
each camper will locate early signs of 
health defects and enable preventive 
measures to be undertaken. 

(2) Morning Dip —This should not be 
compulsory. It should not be allowed 
for certain children who show a ten¬ 
dency to over-tiredness and children 


who are underweight. In any case, it 
should be a dip, and not a swim. 

(3) Teeth —Improper care of the teeth 
during a camp season can result in defi¬ 
nite damage and may break a routine 
which has been established at home. 

(4) Airing of Beds —This is more im¬ 
portant in tents and summer cabins 
than in a city home. The cleanliness 
and changing of bed linen is a preven¬ 
tive factor in such diseases as impetigo. 
A bed-wetter will not be able to hide 
this trouble if airing of beds is enforced. 

(5) Clothing —In early morning, cloth¬ 
ing should be heavier than at any other 
hour of the day, particularly after a 
morning dip. Sweaters and coats can 
be discarded after breakfast if the 
weather is warm. 

(6) Su?i-Tan —This should be acquired 
gradually. The skin should be covered 
before you think that a burn can start. 
The time of exposure can be increased 
each day. 

(7) Fatigue —This is one of the most 
important things to avoid. Excessive 
tiredness over a period of time can do 
a great deal to decrease the benefits of 
camping. When present, it increases 
the risk of infections. Prevention of 
fatigue is most importast during the 
first and the last week of camp. It 
requires some study on the part of the 
staff to pick out those children with 
low tolerance to certain activity. The 
exercise tolerance for each individual 
is variant. 

(8) Rest Periods —The rest hour after 
lunch and the early morning period 
before the rising bell are important 
times for supervision. Bedtime should 
not be a “bedlam”. The last half hour 
of the evening program should tone off 
to provide a suitable frame of mind for 
sleep. An evening program which ends 
with a “bang” or is late in ending is a 
failure from a preventive medical view. 


1 l 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1949 


(9) Swimming —Long swims of dis¬ 
tance or time should be discouraged, as 
they serve no useful purpose and might 
produce physical harm. Diving is not 
desirable for campers with a tendency 
to frequent colds and sinus trouble. 

(10) Hot Bath —At least once a week 
is an essential for all young children. 
It is a good preventive for all ages 
against skin infection. 

(11) Towels —A clean towel for each 
camper is necessary; towels should not 
be shared. 

(12) Mealtime —A child at camp needs 
a balanced diet more than at home, as 
he is more active. Behaviour at meal¬ 
time is important in determining his 
mental and physical health. Loss of 
appetite should be regarded as an early 
sign of some upset (mental or physi¬ 
cal). Loss of appetite often marks the 
onset of an illness. Dining room “at¬ 
mosphere” will, in some individuals, 
affect appetite and digestion. 

(13) Canoe Trips — Inspection for 
minor cuts, scrapes, slivers, etc., is more 
important while away from medical 
help. Instructions in first-aid treatment 
suitable for possible emergencies in the 
individual camp, should be studied and 
taught by the camp physician before 
trips are sent out. 

(14) First Aid Kits and Remedies — 
These can be packed away. The coun¬ 
selor can point out that the camp pro¬ 
vides the necessary equipment. In this 
way the medical staff will be consulted 
early for all minor cuts, etc. 

(15) Laxatives —The bringing of laxa¬ 
tives by campers from home should be 
discouraged. The diet should be regu¬ 
lated to take care of proper elimination. 

(16) Riding — Injuries while riding 
horseback, such as cuts, wounds and 
scrapes, are most important and should 
be reported to the medical staff at once. 


STAFF MEETINGS 

Health conferences at intervals dur¬ 
ing the camp season can do much to 
foster close co-operation between staff 
and medical personnel. General camp 
health program as well as the health 
of individual campers can be discussed. 

The idea of prevention in the camp 
health program can be profitably 
brought up at crucial periods during 
the camp season. For example, the first 
and last weeks are the periods when 
fatigue is most evident. 

While health must be a major con¬ 
sideration in the program at all times, 
it must become a basic reality of the 
everyday life of the camp rather than 
existing as a self-conscious, specialized 
aspect of camp activity. Health should 
be practiced rather than preached; and 
its ultimate aim should be not how 
much children know about it, but the 
place they give it in their daily lives. 


Reprints of this article may he se¬ 
cured from the office of the Ontario 
Camping Association , 236 Bloor St. W., 
Toronto. Price 10 cents. 



12 


Canadian Camping 


Travelling 


Tight 


STUART L. THOMPSON 


Now that the canoe trip season is 
upon us again, there are probably 
thousands of campers all over the con¬ 
tinent making plans for the trip that 
will go down in their memories as the 
high point of the summer of 1949. 
Undoubtedly the preparing of a list 
of things to take in the way of equip¬ 
ment—grub and incidentals—will come 
in for much consideration. Rightly so, 
for a little thought given to preparation 
goes most of the way in insuring a suc¬ 
cessful trip. 

I have often wondered if the value of 
each item on this list of things to take 
on the trip is duly weighed. Do you 
really need all that is on that list? Look 
over it carefully and see if there are 
not things that you can do without, and 
some that can be made to do the work 
of two or even three different things 
on the list. It is true you are going 
on a holiday and I am a firm believer 
in comfort. But remember that camp¬ 
ing, whether stationary or moving on 



Camp Temagami 


the trail with a pack-horse, or on the 
portage with a canoe, is a life Lvcd 
under simple conditions, simpler by far 
than we civilized folks of the twentieth 
century are accustomed to living, and 
every article taken must find its place 
in the outfit. 

I never realized until I had embarked 
on my first canoe trip what a burden 
the host of things on a long list could 
become. My companion had been on 
one previous trip and naturally I relied 
on his judgment and list. I wonder 
now where we put it all in that twelve- 
foot birchbark canoe. I shall always 
look back with fond memories to that 
trip—but oh, the things we did not 
need to take, and how much they added 
to our cares and work. 

Three years later I fell in with an¬ 
other pal, whom I shall call “Dave”, who 
proposed a canoe trip for the following 
summer. Like myself, he had only been 
on one other trip, but I soon realized 
that I was in the hands of a resource- 


Toronto , Canada , June , 1949 


13 




ful, self-reliant camper who had been 
trained in a different school. As we 
compared our lists of equipment in ad¬ 
vance, I was surprised and gratified to 
see the nonchalant way in which Dave 
eliminated one thing after another. 
Listen to him: “We don’t need an axe, 
we have a camp hatchet. We don’t want 
bread, it is bulky and goes stale—hard¬ 
tack takes its place. We’ll not take 
guns—they are heavy, risky, need con¬ 
stant care and cleaning, and mean 
hauling ammunition. And why table 
knives with a hunting knife on your 
belt.” And so he went on deleting the 
list. Good old Dave! I learned on that 
trip how one could camp like a real 
woodsman. 

It was not an easy trip, but we were 
young and tough and enthusiastic. To 
this day I read over my diary and live 
all its joys over again. Yes, and I even 
laugh at the little troubles and hard¬ 
ships we suffered—and what canoe trip 
has not troubles? We were gone two 
weeks through virgin forest of Northern 
Ontario, travelling lakes and rivers and 
portages. For days we saw no one and 
only rarely did we meet another party. 

We went with only one of each item 
of clothing — sweater, shirt, trousers, 
sox and moccasins, and without hats. 
We took no tent—^at night we slept out 
under the stars and if it rained, we slept 
in large waterproof bags which were al¬ 
so used to take care of the grub. Thus 
those bags served for tent, sleeping- 
bags and dunnage-bags. We took no 
bread—hardtack instead. We caught 
fish in abundance, which we broiled 
over a charcoal fire on toasters, thus 
eliminating a frying pan. We carried 
neither bacon not flapjack flour, and 
did not miss them. We had no lantern, 
because at night we sat about the camp¬ 
fire (there were no such things as 
flashlights in those days). Dave knew 
the country; and neither compass nor 
map was needed for the whole hundred 
miles or so. 


For grub we ate porridge cooked in 
tin pails, dried fruit, hardtack, mush¬ 
rooms which we gathered and stewed 
in condensed milk, an abundance of 
fresh fish (bass and salmon and trout) 
broiled in steaks on the toaster, frogs’ 
legs occasionally, and huckleberries and 
raspberries, fresh picked almost any 
place we looked. 

Oh, it was a rough, hard trip! De¬ 
cidedly back to nature, but we enjoyed 
it. Under Dave’s resourceful leader¬ 
ship, I learned how to camp with what 
we had, and what was more important, 
what to leave at home . 

When, on rare occasion, we met the 
members of another party, they mar¬ 
velled at the compactness of our outfit 
—two small packs and a nest of pails, 
that was all! “Gee! you’re travelling 
light”, they would remark. Away down 
in one of those packs Dave would have 
two or three books—a botany, a bird 
book, a star map. We were cmpletely 
out of touch with the world, but Dave 
believed in being in touch with the 
world of nature. 

Well, that was all over thirty years 
ago. Dave and I had many later trips, 
and I have had more trips since under 
different circumstances and with vari¬ 
ous companions. Things have altered 
so that I now take a few of the things 
Dave eliminated. But the basic prin¬ 
ciple remains as I learned it: there are 
a lot of things you really don't need 
and which prove cumbersome and a 
worry throughout the trip . 

I once listened to a “camper” lecture 
in a camp on equipment. He had a 
dunnage-bag full of ideas, which he 
pulled out triumphantly as he talked. 
I recall only a few of them: 

1. A canvas wash basin to be set up 
in a tripod for washing hands and face. 
Why? Is there not a whole lake at 
hand? 


14 


Canadian Camping 



2. A fly for the tent roof. Why? Only 
another thing to string up and blow 
down. 

3. A padded collar for the shoulders 
when portaging a canoe. Why? Your 
sweater and the other fellow’s rolled up 
one on each shoulder are far thicker 
and softer, and can be used as sweaters 
as well. 

4. A cushion for a pillow at night and 
to kneel on while paddling in day. 
Why? A sweater will do for both. 

5. Poles for the tent. Why? Are there 
not trees in abundance everywhere? 

6. A cushion mattress to be blown up 
at night. Why? Is there not lots ol 
balsam, spruce, and other things for 
bedding? 

And so on endlessly — pots, pails, 
dishes, ovens, pans, knives, forks, axes, 


etc., and in many cases spares of this 
and that in case something got lost! 
And pitch to mend the canoe, needle 
and thread and buttons to mend clothes, 
etc., etc. We mended any tears and 
rips in clothes with fishing-line and 
when we puctured a hole through the 
bottom of Dave’s canoe we effectually 
fixed it with balsam, gum off the trees 
ten feet away, stuck in place by a piece 
of cloth cut from a grub-bag. 

So I think at this season it is well to 
look over those camp lists carefully with 
the thought, “what can I do without, 
consistent with comfort?” It has been 
said that a poor workman always 
blames his tools. In the same way a 
good, capable, resourceful woodsman 
makes the fewest tools do the most for 
him. Was it not that veteran woods¬ 
man, Teddy Roosevelt, who said: 
“With what you have, where you are”? 



Photoyruph y 

in CAMP 

Colin S. Farmer 


S’ncc camp days arc among the hap¬ 
piest days in a boy’s or a girl’s life, it 
is natural for every camper to want to 
re-live camp experiences again and 
agam during the following school year 
and for yean to come. Nothing can 
bring these happy days back to mind 
quite as well as can a collection of good 
pictures. 

It is an excellent idea to have some 
member of the camp staff who follows 
photography as a hobby and who has 
a good camera with the necessary tripod 
and flashlight equipment to record the 
big events in camp life for the con¬ 
venience of all the campers. He can 
sell these pictures at a reasonable price 
to nearly every person in the camp be¬ 
cause they represent the activities in 
which the whole camp works together. 
Besides, the cameras owned by the 
campers cannot usually make these 
pictures very successfully. These acti¬ 
vities include plays, stunt nights, coun¬ 
cil ring, circuses, regattas and possibly 
group meetings when some special 
guest visits a camp fire. Group pictures 
of the staff or a section of the camp 
can hardly be done with the small 
cameras used by the majority of the 
campers and staff. 

For the camper or counselor who is 
bringing his own camera with him to 
camp, I would like to suggest that he 
should have some competent person 
check it over before he leaves home. A 
hole no larger than a pin point in the 


bellows is not easy for the amateur to 
detect, but it can ruin every picture by 
letting light into the camera. If one 
roll of film comes back with streaks or 
areas of light where they should not be, 
the camera should be examined when 
there is no film in it, by opening up the 
back and looking at the inside of the 
bellows, holding the camera up towards 
the light, so that any tiny hole could 
be seen. Temporary repairs may be 
made in camp by fastening a piece of 
adhesive over the hole before another 
film is used. 

The lens and the shutter must also 
be in the best of shape. A dirty lens 
will never produce clear pictures any 
more than a dirty pair of glasses or a 
dirty automobile windshield will permit 
a person to see clearly what lies in front. 
A camera lens should be cleaned with 
the same care as a pair of glasses. But 
some cameras have four surfaces on 
the lenses and the inner ones may be 
reached only by screwing the lenses out 
of their mounts. Clean them with a very 
soft, lintless cloth and be certain that 
they are put back exactly where they 
were at first. The shutter must be sure 
to work whenever the shutter release 
is pressed. Since the better shutters are 
about as complicated as a watch, it 
would be unwise for the amateur to 
try to effect repairs when they do not 
work. Let some regular repair man put 
the shutter in good working order if 
anything goes wrong. 


16 


Canadian Camping 


In choosing a new camera for the 
beginner to use in camp it would be 
wise to select a fairly simple and inex¬ 
pensive type. The reason for this is 
that there are so few adjustments to be 
watched on a simple camera like the 
box cameras that the inexperienced 
photographer is not likely to become 
confused and make mistakes. A good 
box camera about six-sixteen size is a 
splendid type for the young or inex¬ 
perienced camper. If the camper is 
more experienced as a photographer, 
he will possibly want a camera which 
will do pictures which the simpler 
cameras are not intended to do. Since 
these campers already know what they 
want in a camera and are acquainted 
with the various makes and prices I 
need not offer them any advice in this 
brief article. A larger lens permits the 
taking of pictures in weaker k’ght, but 
it calls for much more careful judging 
of distance if the pictures are to be in 
clear focus. 

Almost all of the pictures which the 
campers will take during the summer 
will be taken out of doors during bright 
weather. They must remember that 


all pictures are made by the aid of light 
and that even the fastest modern film 
cannot make a picture unless it re¬ 
ceives sufficient light. A counselor who 
usually gets good snapshots with his 
own camera can give the beginner the 
help he may need in this matter of 
lighting. A good plan in taking the 
tent or cabin group, for example, is to 
avoid trying to take the group inside the 
building, but rather to group them 
informally somewhere outside and in¬ 
clude the tent or cabin in the back¬ 
ground if possible. 

Every camper will be anxious to have 
a number of pictures of his special 
camp friends. Most people take better 
pictures if their minds are occupied 
with some activity. Let the young pho¬ 
tographer, therefore, select the most 
appropriate activity and background 
for each of his pictures and then fit his 
subject into it and take the picture. 
The background is very important for 
every picture. Often the background 
should be scarcely noticed. A camper 
with a horse, for example, takes a good 
picture in the stable doorway with a 
background so dark that it may show 



Camp Fine Crest 


Toronto , Canada , June , 1949 


17 



nothing inside the building. A group 
in a sailboat preparing for a sail may 
be taken looking down from the diving 
tower where the only background is 
water. A diver taken from a low angle 
may show him in mid-air with only a 
clear sky for background. A canoe trip 
group preparing a meal may show only 
rocks and trees in the distance. 

It would be a good idea for some 
counselor to collect a scrap book of 
interesting camp pictures including pic¬ 
tures clipped from magazines, news¬ 
papers, or from camp booklets, to give 
campers some idea of what makes a 
good picture. One friend of mine who 
has made a great many good pictures 
likes to sketch his idea of a picture 
with pencil on paper before he goes 
out to take it with his camera. A snap¬ 
shot becomes a real picture when the 
subject matter in it is nicely balanced 
and attractively lighted. 

Among the most prized pictures 


which the writer has in his collection 
from his summers in camp are: indi¬ 
vidual younger campers doing some 
painstaking work in the workshop, the 
activity around the diving tower at 
swim period with a good white cloud 
background, the ornamental swimming 
class at work, junior campers making 
“Pine Cone gardens” on the sandy 
beach, the “Chief” in costume before 
the totem pole, the Sunday parade in 
white down the hill from the outdoor 
chapel, the numerous pictures out 
across the lake towards the sunset, 
vistas through the trees over the lake 
including a sailboat or two, the cooking 
of outdoor meals, small groups in 
special activities like circus sideshows, 
archery, horseback riding. Almost every 
special activity in the camp programme 
will suggest a few good picture making 
opportunities. All the young photo¬ 
grapher needs to do is to recognize these 
opportunities and take advantage of 
them. 



Camp Oolahwan 


18 


Canadian Camping 





Quebec Camps 


Agnes Knox Mutchler, 

Director, Junior League Camp, Montreal 


The mountain and small lakes of 
Quebec have been calling to camp 
minded people for many years. Many 
camps were started in that era when 
fresh air was supposed to be so bene¬ 
ficial as to overcome the ills of primi¬ 
tive privies, milk without benefit of 
Pasteur and a modicum of science 
generally. A few of these still survive 
but for the most part electricity, high 
sanitation standards and sound pro¬ 
gram mark Quebec camps today. The 
complete loveliness of the Quebec ter¬ 
rain has not changed and good roads 
are constantly opening up new camping 
areas. 

The tales told by those pioneers of 
the early camping period are simply 
amazing. One gets a picture of bloom¬ 
er girls and gentlemen in starched col¬ 
lars lugging great timbers through the 
wild woods, harrassed by bears and 
wolves, mosquitoes and black flies and 
personally hammering together the 
shelters and equipment. Swollen and 
bitten, the non-profit camp people 
wrestled with pianos and other furni¬ 
ture weighing tons, too outmoded for 
the city dwelling. In spite of the hard¬ 
ships these early camp enthusiasts were 
convinced of the necessity for a camp¬ 
ing experience in a world which was 
becoming mechanised until the human 
element was pressed beyond endurance. 
Some day these stories will be written 
and may they appear, at least in part, 
in Canadian Camping. 


Today in Quebec we have forty-five 
permanent camps registered with the 
Quebec Camping Section. Twenty-nine 
of these are non profit camps. They are 
of two types, those which find their 
money in public contributions and 
those whose fees cover operating ex¬ 
penses. A few very short term camps 
survive, but for the most part two 
weeks is the shortest camping experi¬ 
ence offered. Camp Lewis, under the 
direction of Mr. Wylie, offers good 
camping to five hundred boys for two 
weeks or longer each year. The Junior 
League Camp gives fun to one hundred 
girls for three weeks, three times each 
summer. Chapleau, which is Quebec’s 
Bolton, looks after Mothers and chil¬ 
dren. The divisions and activities of 
this Camp would seem to require the 
skill and experience of a circus manager 
when it comes to organization. The 
Mother who returned post haste to 
Montreal when she discovered that hot 
and cold water was not laid on, was 
probably a rate type, but Miss Nan Vail, 
the Director, has many tales of Camp 
Chapleau which will make fine reading 
some day. 

The date and origin of many of the 
early camps is even now clouded in 
antiquity. Certainly a boys’ camp spon¬ 
sored by the Y.M.C.A. of Montreal in 
1893 and called Otoreke was among the 
earliest. Kanawana, at present directed 
by Roy Locke, Vice-President of the 
Quebec Section, had a mysterious birth 


Toronto, Canada, June, 1949 


19 



about this time under the same sponsor¬ 
ship. The Y.W.C.A. Gamp Oolahwan, 
under the vigorous leadership of Mary 
Edgar, was hewn from the woods in 
1919. Oolahwan has its own lake and 
six hundred acres. It is directed by our 
President, Diana Cumner, has mar¬ 
velous woodland facilities and a flexible 
programme in keeping with the most 
advanced theory of camping. It ob¬ 
viously was not all beer and skittles for 
any of the camps in the early days. The 
Junior League Camp was started more 
than twenty-five years ago through the 
pluck and determination of Miss L'ght- 
hall of Montreal, on family property 
near St. Marguerites. I am sure there 
are many stories of early camps that 
I have not been able to collect, but 
maybe the fact that they are not men¬ 
tioned in this article will lead some of 
the pioneers to put their experiences 
on paper. 

The Quebec Camping Association 
had its origin in the thirties. It is an 
original member of the Canadian 
Camping Association. This Section 
tries to keep in close touch with all 
camps in the Province. This is ex¬ 
tremely difficult, because the registered 
camps for the most part are in the two 
areas, the Laurentians and the Eastern 
Townships. Certainly the magnificent 
St. Lawrence River, broadening out to 
the sea, should offer superb camping 
facilities, but as yet little is known to 
the Quebec Section of camping facili¬ 
ties in that area. 

Every effort is being made to bring 
the Quebec Camps up to the best stan¬ 
dards in health, sanitation and pro¬ 
gramme. The Section recognises the 
need for knowledgable staff and coun¬ 
selors, and sponsors many training 
courses for those who would be Leaders 
in this field. It has backed the appoint¬ 
ment of year-round Directors for non¬ 
profit camps, recognising the need for 
continuity of program in camps and 
winter training. Another element has 
entered here, and that is the need for 


winterising camps so that many more 
people may enjoy that invigorating 
winter sport of skiing. In a Province 
almost as famous as the Alps for luxury 
skiing, it seems ridiculous that any 
camps are closed to ordinary people 
who would love to zip over the wooded 
hills and mountain slopes during the 
long winter months. 

The swimming section of the Red 
Cross has worked closely with the 
camping group. Last year hundreds of 
young people passed the Red Cross 
tests and all winter practical courses in 
health and water safety have proven 
a boon to those who would be leaders 
on Waterfront. 

The Executive of the Quebec Section 
is drawn from all types of Camps, both 
private and non-profit and a great deal 
of time is absorbed by this voluntary 
effort. In spite of all the work done, it 
is obvious that only the surface has 
been scratched. Mr. A1 Dodds of the 
Central Y.M.C.A. is the Secretary and 
would like nothing better than to be 
snowed under by mail from Camps. 
Only by exchanging ideas and sugges¬ 
tions with all the Camps in the Pro¬ 
vince can we really fulfill the function 
of the Provincial Section.

20 


Canadian Camping 


The Editor Comments 


For the most part, the children who 
come to our camps are boys and girls 
from the crowded cities. The world 
they know best is one of pavements, 
brick walls, street cars and super mar¬ 
kets. It is a far cry from the Canada 
our pioneer grandparents helped to 
clear and settle, and the land with 
which country children are still more 
or less familiar. 

This fact was brought vividly to my 
attention one summer when a twelve- 
year-old camper hesitated to strike a 
match at a campcraft fire-building 
demonstration. She said: “I have never 
lit a fire before in all my life. We use 
only electricity in our apartment.” My 
thoughts flew back to a childhood 
crammed with such thrilling adventures 
as a “sugaring-off” party around a huge 
bonfire, when the maple forest was lit 
up with the flames. I thought, too, of 
the contrast between apartment life and 
our long summer holidays of unorgan¬ 
ized fun—shore picnics, berry picking, 
fishing trips, when the whole country¬ 
side was a friendly place to explore 
“on one’s own”. There came a sudden 
realization of how far city children 
are from those “horse and buggy days”, 
and how they have definitely been de¬ 
prived of a rich heritage of simple 
pleasures in the vast wonderland of 
the out-of-doors. 

Camping is the Magic Key which can 
open that lost land of enchantment to 
the city boys and girls of today. Beyond 
the smoky horizons of sky-scrapers and 
factory chimneys there are countless 
wooded lakes, winding streams, rolling 
hills, towering mountains and un¬ 


tracked forests. That is Canada! That 
is their heritage! When they sing: “O 
Canada, we stand on guard for thee”, 
they should have a knowledge of and 
a love for that larger land, with a few 
tender memories deep in their hearts 
of “good old camping-out days”, filled 
with happy adventures, comradeship 
and a sense of reverence for the wonder 
of the world in which they live. 

Camping is probably the only ex¬ 
perience we can offer them which will 
acquaint them with some of the ad¬ 
ventures the pioneers had when our 
land was new. They can blaze a trail 
through the woods; they can portage 
their canoes; they can cook over an 
open fire; they can build a balsam bed 
and sleep out all night under the stars. 
They will then realize that these are 
still the experiences of our explorers 
and prospectors and settlers who con¬ 
tinue to push back the frontiers in the 
vast hinterland of our great Dominion. 

If you can learn to love your lakes and 
forests 

Can feel within you: “This belongs 
to me!”; 

Your heart, expanding, will embrace 
your country 

And proudly then you’ll pledge your 
loyalty. 

We must keep before us the high 
objective—more and better camps for 
an increasing multitude of children, 
and as camp leaders, we are justified in 
believing there will be amazing divi¬ 
dends in the producing of better 
Canadians.

A Letter from 


Nutrition Department, 
Canadian Red Cross Society, 
Ontario Division, 

Hello Camp Directors: 

Wc enjoyed meeting many of you in 
February when you visited our exhibit 
at the Ontario Camping Association 
Pow Wow. But we’re sure wc d : dn’t 
meet all of you—so we decided to write 
to you. Wc hope that this letter will 
draw to your attention the importance 
of planning good meals for your 
campers. 

There are four important points 
about CAMP MEALS that should be 
incorporated into your plans for this 
summer’s camp. Remember that: 

1. A camp is as good as the lood it 
serves. 

2. Camp meals require as much care¬ 
ful planning as do meals at home. 

3. Camp meals arc an important part 
of the camp program. They, too, 
assist in the mental and physical 
growth and development of the 
camper. 

4. Camp meals offer a splendid oppor¬ 
tunity for developing good food 
habits. The group spirit of camp 


life encourages boys and girls to 
drink milk, eat vegetables, fruits 
and whole grain products — food 
habits which may very probably 
have been neglected at home. 

Camp Directors, did you know that 
Red Cross nutritionists are available 
to help you and your campers? Upon 
request, a Red Cross nutritionist: 

Will —plan menus for your camp. 

Will —give suggestions for necessary 
kitchen equipment. 

Will —visit your camp if you have no 
dietitian. 

Will —talk to your campers about good 
foods for good health. 

Will —show nutrition films to your 
campers. 

As Camp directors, you may be inter¬ 
ested in having a nutritionist visit your 
camp this summer to help in any or all 
of these five ways. Just write us at 
your earliest convenience—with details 
about your camp, and perhaps tenta¬ 
tive dates for a visit. 

Remember that at camps, all of us 
strive for the same goal—a healthier 
and happier camper! 

May wc hear from you? 

Sincerely, 

RED CROSS NUTRITIONISTS.

NOTES 


SASKATCHEWAN 


front the Provinces 


BRITISH COLUMBIA 

The Camping Association chose 
“Counselor Training” as a major pro¬ 
ject this year, in order to offer special 
service to the camps of British Colum¬ 
bia, and cooperating with the Van¬ 
couver School Board, promoted a 
course from March 28th to May 18th, 
ever) 7 Monday evening. 

One thousand counselor-application 
forms were circulated through the Wo¬ 
men’s Voluntary Bureau to church 
groups, departmental stores and high 
schools, in an effort to create a pool of 
counselors for the use of camps. 

In cooperation with the Red Cross 
Society, the B.C.C.A. is also under¬ 
taking to run a four weeks’ course on 
“Swimming and Water Safety”, from 
April 25th to May 30th. An effort has 
been made this year to raise the stand¬ 
ard of counselors and it is anticipated 
that the methods employed will help 
all concerned to realize a successful 
camping experience this summer. 


ALBERTA 

The Patrol-Leaders’ Training Camp 
of the Girl Guides’ Association will be 
held on the Provincial Campsite at 
Mulhurst, Pidgeon Lake, from July 
14th - 21st. Approximate individual fee 
for the week will be ten dollars. 

The Guiders’ Training Camp will be 
from July 21st- 28th, on the same site. 
The Saskatchewan leaders are joining 
this group. 


The Third Annual Camp Conference 
of the Saskatchewan Camping Associa¬ 
tion was held this- year at the Regina 
Boat Club, May 13th and 14th. 

An interesting plan was worked out 
to have two all-day conferences on a 
Saturday and Sunday, and dove-tailing 
to accommodate everyone. Saturday 
was the “common day” to both con¬ 
ferences. Another unusual and attrac¬ 
tive feature was the offer to supply 
free billets for all out-of-town dele¬ 
gates, and to extend the invitation to 
“anyone interested in — or doing — a 
camp job!” 



Mrs. Pauline Hill, President of the Saskat¬ 
chewan Camping Association; graduate of 
the Margaret Eaton School of Physical 
Education, Toronto; former counselor at 
Glen Bernard Camp, and physical director 
of the Regina Y.W.C.A. Since her marriage, 
Mrs. Hill has devoted a great deal of her 
time to the work of the Saskatchewan 
Camping Association. 


Toronto 3 Canada, June, 1949 


23 


MANITOBA 

The Manitoba Section held its first 
meeting of 1949 on March 23rd, in the 
Y.W.C.A. The nominating committee 
submitted its recommendations and a 
new slate of officers was elected. The 
president is Mr. J. C. Harwood, Mani¬ 
toba Director of the Boy Scout Associa¬ 
tion. 

The status of the Manitoba Section 
as an independent organization in the 
province was discussed. It was decided 
to appoint a committee to investigate 
the constitution, and to suggest 
revisions. 

The new constitution was passed on 
April 6th. At this time too, the Cana¬ 
dian Red Cross Water Safety film, 
taken at the Taylor Statten Camps, 
Algonquin Park, was shown, and proved 
most interesting and informative. 

The Manitoba Section of the C.C.A. 
is planning a Camping Institute, under 
the direction of Professor Alan Klein, 
to take place during the month of May. 
We are anticipating a profitable time 
under Mr. Klein’s practical and able 
guidance. 


QUEBEC 

The Quebec Section arranged a 
training course for counselors for four 
evenings in March. More than one 
hundred counselors registered, repre¬ 
senting all types of camps. Judging from 
the sustained attendance, it was evi¬ 
dent that the kind of intellectual camp 
fare offered was just what was needed 
and appreciated. 

An interesting meeting was arranged 
by Miss Ross of the Social Agencies for 
the non-profit camps. Ten camps were 
invited. While one agrees with Pro¬ 
fessor Klein of Toronto University, that 
camping theory is the same for all types 
of camps, there are certain problems in 
the Welfare Camps connected with ad¬ 


ministration, contacts and personnel, 
which are exclusive to this level. The 
discussion of costs was illuminating. 
The problems of how closely it is pos¬ 
sible for this kind of camp to work with 
the Social Agencies, was extremely help¬ 
ful. A meeting of this group will be 
called again next fall to map out cer¬ 
tain subjects for study, to collect data 
which should have research value and 
generally to pool information and 
review problems. 

The Spring Conference for Coun¬ 
selors was held on May 13th and 14th. 


PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND 

“The Island” has had a Leadership 
Training Camp for the past two years. 
These camps were sponsored by the 
Camping Association. Counsellors and 
counsellors-in-training represented the 
Y.M.C.A., Knights of Columbus, Girl 
Guides, Boy Scouts and several church 
camps. The Canadian Red Cross par¬ 
ticipated in this project and conducted 
a Swimming and Water Safety Instruc¬ 
tors’ School in conjunction with the 
Leadership Training Course. 


FORUM ON “LEISURE” 

A National Recreation Forum is to 
be held on or about October 20th, in 
Montreal. This Forum is to be spon¬ 
sored by eight National organizations 
and will be a substitute for the Cana¬ 
dian Recreation Congress. The topic 
of the Forum will be: “Leisure—a 
National Issue”. This subject will stress 
the need in Canada for recreational re¬ 
sources, including camping. 

It is expected that the Canadian 
Camping Association will hold its An¬ 
nual Meeting either immediately prior 
to this Forum, or immediately after¬ 
ward.

Camp Winnebagoe Says . . . 


We thought that you might be interested 
in learning how pleased we are with the 
satisfaction that we have obtained from 
Maplex Plastic Ware. 

As you are no doubt aware, we pur¬ 
chased a small quantity of this as an 
experiment a few years ago, and it proved 
so satisfactory that we have completely 
discarded our vitrified ware for plastic 
dishes. 

Not only has our breakage been reduced 
to one quarter of what it was previously, 
but the convenience to the young people 
that wait on our tables is exceptionally 
encouraging, as there is no comparison in 
the weight of the plastic dishes and the 
old-fashioned chinawares. 

Our Camp colours are green and grey, 
and the green dishes on our grey table 
tops provides a most attractive and invit¬ 
ing colour contrast. It gives the tables a 
"New Look" with this modern type of 
tableware instead of the antiquated 
restaurant type. 

Chipping and cracking of china dishes is 
most dangerous, as health authorities have 
proven that the germs that accumulate in 
chips and cracks very seldom are com¬ 
pletely eliminated in any type of washing 
facilities, no matter how up-to-date the 
equipment may be or what type of solu¬ 
tions are used in the washing. Maplex 
Plastic Ware almost eliminates this hazard. 

We appreciate the courteous and effi¬ 
cient service you have afforded us in the 
past, and anticipate a continuance of 
similar relationships in the future. 

Very sincerely, 

CAMP WINNEBAGOE LIMITED. 

Sadie W. Danson, Director.

BOOK REVIEWS 

THE SPORT OF ORIENTEERING, 
by S. Hedenstrom and B. Kjellstrom; 
published by Silva Limited, Toronto; 

p.p. 120. 

This is an English translation of a 
Swedish text describing a sport which 
has been extensively developed in Swe¬ 
den over the period of the last thirty 
years. The sport is really hiking dressed 
up to make it a bit more than that. 
The dressing up should re-establish this 
fine activity and recreation in a country 
which has latterly become enamoured 
of riding something. 

Orienteering requires the use of a 
compass and a detailed map. A special 
compass housing and gadget for steering 
by, have been developed. This kind 
of compass is now available in Canada 
from the Silva Company, Toronto. The 
sport can be purely recreational as a 
method of finding your way around, 
walking, cycling, riding, paddling or 
skiing. How to make any of these com¬ 
petitive is described in the text, which 
is well supplied with illustratons. 

The author, Bom Kjellstrom, was in 
Canada last summer and introduced 
the sport at several places. A fine 
coloured movie is available from the 
National Film Society, Ottawa. 

A CAMP AQUATIC PROGRAM 
(Third Edition), by Richard H. 
Bearse and Sidney C. Hazel ton; price 
$2.25 plus 10c for mailing and 
handling. Copies obtainable from 
Prof. S. C. Hazel ton, 7 Dana Road, 
Hanover, N.H. 

This is a handbook for the water¬ 
front director. The camp director 
would be well advised to read it, too, 
not ony for its specific help in planning 
the waterfront layout, but because of 
its clear statements in regard to policy, 
safety, etc. 

It contains a job analysis for the 
waterfront men, lesson plans for teach¬ 
ing swimming, boating and canoeing, 
a suggested waterfront policy, time¬ 


tables, record sheets and charts. It also 
has a survey of the requirements before, 
during and after camp. It deals with 
all aspects of swimming and boating, 
functional, recreational, competitive 
and ornamental. It also has detailed 
plans with diagrams for buildings and 
wharfs. These are in sufficient variety 
to meet all needs. It is sound and 
business-like in its approach. 

THE HANDBOOK OF DAY-CAMP¬ 
ING, by Mabel Jobe; Association 
Press, obtainable in Canada from the 
G. R. Welch Co., Limited, 1149 King 
Street West, Toronto; published 
April 1, 1949; pp. 276; price $3.50. 

Throughout the country, many social 
agencies and churches are increasingly 
providing hundreds of thousands of 
children with camping experiences at 
home — in the playgrounds — public 
parks, etc. Here is a detailed blueprint 
on how to use day-camping to enrich 
children’s lives, to build a happy, co¬ 
operative way of living, and to meet the 
social, emotional and play needs of 
children without complicated organiza¬ 
tion or elaborate equipment. 

Nothing is omitted—from how to 
get started to appraising on-going pro¬ 
grams. The author shows how to select 
a site, provide for health and safety, 
select workers, train a staff, counsel 
children, etc. Complete programs and 
daily schedules are outlined; detailed 
menus and instructions for cooking- 
out are given; nature studies are em¬ 
phasized; inventories of equipment and 
supplies are suggested for new and 
established camps. All of the material 
is basic program material for those who 
help children to play and learn. 

The author started day-camping in 
the District of Columbia. Many years 
ago Mrs. Jobe borrowed some tools, got 
a fire permit and started some fun with 
a few neighbourhood children on an 
empty lot. Mrs. Jobe has literally spent 
her lifetime camping, teaching children, 
and teaching camping: she has helped 
train thousands of teachers and leaders. 


Toronto, Canada , June , 1949

THE BOOK OF CAMPING, by Ro¬ 
bert Rubin; Association Press, obtain¬ 
able in Canada from the G. R. Welch 
Company, Limited, 1149 King Street 
West, Toronto; published March 1, 
1949; pp. 160; price, cloth, $2.25. 

In a simple, readable way, this book 
covers every aspect of camp house¬ 
keeping, programs, administration and 
leadership. As camping has developed 
to its present established position in 
Canadian education, recreation, and 
child-development programs, a varied 
literature has developed on its many 
phases. This is one of the first attempts 
to provide beginners, leaders-in-train- 
ing and experienced camp directors 
with a concise, handy, Baedeker to 
camping. 

Just about everything essential is 
here: what camping is; job analysis for 
the counselor and his pre-camp and in- 
service training; camp curricula in 
nature, crafts, music, typical camp 
schedules; rainy-day programs; the 
camp budget; kitchen and food con¬ 
trols; menus for two weeks; song lists; 
cabin mail charts; and forms and blanks 
for all operations.

The Camp Directors Workshop and

to Ellsworth Jaeger’s already extensive 
library of books on camping and the 
out-of-doors. It is a compact and useful 
presentation of camp-fire practices, 
ceremonies, games, songs and dances 
mainly on the Indian Council theme. 
Mr. Jaeger adds many of his own 
special contributions particularly in the 
field of nature lore and Indian tales, 
and in his suggested methods of making 
the many articles than can be used in 
this type of Council Ring program such 
as: masks, Indian costumes, drums, 
rattles, totems and emblems. Here is 
the basis for a worth-while and intrinsic 
craft program at camp. The volume 
is rich in Indian designs. 

The picturesque and graphic illus¬ 
trations bring this volume to life even 
for the casual reader. By representing 
successive stages of a theme, they tell 
a continuous and complete story — 
sometimes even more entertainingly and 
succinctly than on the printed page. 
Both illustrations and reading matter 
appeal to the reader’s imagination, 
stimulating him to creative effort. He 
is constantly aware of the smell of wood 
smoke, of Indian figures performing 
primitive dances in the firelight; of 
Indian braves in council combat and 
of the dim figure of the teller-of-tales 
weaving his spell. This volume presents 
tested material—but it also weaves a 
spell.

train themselves first in methods and 
techniques of staff training. The dele¬ 
gates to the “Pow Wow” heartily en¬ 
dorsed the suggestions, and the Direc¬ 
tors Seminar was born. 

The Canadian Camping Association 
proposed that the Ontario Camping 
Association run the Seminar, but open 
it to camp directors in all other pro¬ 
vinces in Canada. The proposal was 
adopted, and it has now become a 
National Seminar, planned and organ¬ 
ized by the Ontario Section. Professor 
Charles Hendry, well known for his 
work at the National Camp Training 
Centre, was selected as the Director, 
and Dr. Dimock has agreed to partici¬ 
pate and conduct the sessions on super¬ 
vision. 

The Seminar will be held at Camp 
Wabi-Kon, Timagami, Ontario, from 
September 6th to September 11th, with 
sessions taking place September 7 th, 
8th, 9th and 10th. It will afford an 
opportunity for demonstrations, lec¬ 
tures, discussions and work shop tech¬ 
niques in all phases of supervision and 
training. It is expected that the partici¬ 
pants in the Seminar will take an active 
part in helping to raise the standards of 
camping throughout Canada, and there¬ 
by bring another improvement in our 
excellent and growing camping move¬ 
ment.

HEATED WATER SUPPLY 

A simple suggestion for heating water 
is illustrated in the sketch below, and 
comes from the Bulletin of the Saskat¬ 
chewan Camping Association. 



A large tank (300 gallons) placed 
on a trestle built about seven feet from 
ground level and a jacket heater is 
installed right under it. This heater is 
kept going twenty-four hours a day and 
supplies the camp with all the hot water 
required for dishes, galley and washing 
uses. The tank is filled by a small gaso¬ 
line engine pump, costing about one 
hundred dollars. This pump could 
draw from a well, river or lake, as 
desired. It is recommended that a 
qualified plumber be consulted re safety 
valves, etc. 

PIERRE’S “WISDOM” 

Pierre likes going about the bush and 
over the lakes and rivers guided by his 
sense of direction. Last summer Pierre 
was shown a gadget, developed in

Sweden, that took his fancy. It is a 
compass in a special housing. In Swe¬ 
den it is used in the sport of Orienteer¬ 
ing, which is a kind of cross country 
running. This special compass and a 
good map of the terrain are used to¬ 
gether, to get the hiker, runner, pad- 
dlicr or skier from one point to another 
the shortest and quickest way. In 
Canada the compass may be obtained 
from the Silva Company, Toronto, and 
the maps from the provincial and 
federal governments. Maps drawn on 
an inch to a mile scale are best. 

Pierre may be a lazy fellow but he 
has another like and it is for the fifteen 
foot canvas covered canoe for boys’ 
camps. The younger campers are able 
to control the canoe more easily while 
they are learning to paddle single. On 
trips it is big enough to carry the load 
and be handled with greater case, too. 

Tarpaulins are useful things on trips. 
While paddling they can be used to pro¬ 
tect the packs. At camp sites they can 
be used to sit on when the ground is 
wet. They take the place of a tent for 
night protection. The tarpaulin, ac¬ 


cording to that bush wanderer Pierre, is 
easily put up, means carrying less gear, 
and it stands the handling and banging 
about, better than a tent. Where the 
flies are bad the tarpaulin permits the 
use of mosquito bars. 

PAINTING BY SPRAYING 

For those camps who are fortunate 
enough to have electric power available, 
it is suggested that a worthwhile piece 
of equipment is a paint spraying ma¬ 
chine. These are available in various 
sizes at reasonable prices. The lowest 
priced diaphragm type of compressor 
is quite suitable for many jobs around 
camp, particularly painting canoes and 
boats of all kinds. It does a smooth job 
and gets into odd corners, around ribs, 
etc., where a brush will not. Moreover, 
the amount of time saved over ordinary 
methods is amazing. These machines 
are used with ordinary prepared paint 
and will also handle stain, etc. Follow 
your hardware man’s advice in selecting 
a machine of proper capacity for the 
jobs you have in mind.

BLUEBERRY DUMPLINGS 

This is a very satisfactory (and satis¬ 
fying) dessert for a large group on a 
cook-out. 

Ingredients: 

Dehydrated blueberries. 

Water and sugar. 

Tea-Bisk or its equivalent. 

Milk to mix. 

Equipment: 

A pot with a large base circum¬ 
ference, and a tightly fitting cover. 

A mixing spoon, long-handled. 

A pot or bowl to mix the dumplings. 

A fire to fit the large pot. This should 
be a steady fire but not an intense 
one. 

Method: Put your blueberries into the 
pot and add the required amount of 
sugar according to the recipe. Add the 
water also, and increase it by one quar¬ 
ter more. Bring to the boil. Mix the 
tea biscuits, adding a little more milk 
than required. Drop by spoonfuls, not 
large ones, onto the hot blueberries. 
Cover tightly and cook twelve to fifteen 
minutes. 

SHANTY BEANS! 

Did you ever hear of shanty-baked 
beans! You can bake them yourself, 
and once you do, canned beans will 
never taste the same. 

First, parboil your beans on a slow 
fire and let them simmer for a couple 
of hours. Dig a hole in the sand, about 
twice the size of the bean pot. Line the 
hole with flat stones. Grease the bottom 
of the bake pot. If you have a raw 
Spanish onion, lay slices on the floor of 
the pot and pour in half the beans. 
Cover these with a layer of salt pork 
(bacon if you have none other—fatty 
as possible). Then pour in the other 
half of the beans and cover with water. 
Put in a tablespoon of molasses or 
brown sugar, or white sugar if that’s 
all you have. Cover the pot tightly, and 
weight it down with a heavy stone so 
that no steam can escape to let the 
beans steam dry. Shovel a pail full of 
coals from the hot fire into the bottom 
of the hole, set in your pot, and fill up 
the sides of the hole all around it. 
Cover over all with hot wood ashes.

training courses will be held again,

be extended and enriched, and of 
greater variety. 

The girls’ courses will be held at

courses, at Bark Lake Gamp in Hali-

August 2-23. 

Subsidies are continued and increased 
as follows: 

(a) 50c per camper remaining 6-8 con¬ 
secutive nights;

consecutive nights;

more consecutive nights.

$1.75 per day, and still qualify for 
a subsidy. 

(c) Subsidies arc available only to 
camps operated in Ontario, by 
Ontario organizations, for Ontario 
boys and girls.

THE CAMPER AND THE 
BIRTHDAY SUIT 

Once there was a camper 
Whose first letter to her home 
Amazed her doting parents 

And inspired this little “pome”. 

(She wrote:) 

Dear Mum and Dad: Got here o.k. 

Please send a box of food. 

My cabin mates inform me 

There is swimming “a la nude”. 
They say my bathing suit won’t do. 

It’s not the kind they wear. 

Please buy for me a “Birthday Suit”, 
And rush it here by air. 

—M.S.E. 

Counselor : “It might be a hemlock 
or a spruce or a balsam. I’m not quite 
sure.” 

Camper : (later) : “What kind of a 
tree is this one?” 

Counselor : “I think it’s an ash, or a 
beech or perhaps an elm.” 

Camper : “I hope you don’t mind me 
asking so many questions.” 

Counselor : “Why, of course not. It’s 
the only way you’ll ever learn any¬ 
thing.” 

A SERENADE AT CAMP 

He stood on the bridge at midnight, 
Disturbing my sweet repose. 

The “He” was a large mosquito: 

The “Bridge” was the bridge of my 
nose!
